column6: Je mange du pain le matin.
column7: I eat bread in the morning.
column8: It is often used with the partitive article: du pain means "some bread".

column6: Je voudrais un verre d'eau.
column7: I would like a glass of water.
column8: It is feminine and the plural is eaux.

column6: Il boit du lait chaud.
column7: He drinks hot milk.
column8: It is masculine: le lait. The final t is silent.

column6: J'aime le fromage français.
column7: I like French cheese.
column8: It is masculine, like Italian formaggio.

column6: Elle ne mange pas de viande.
column7: She does not eat meat.
column8: Viande means meat; it does not mean food in general.

column6: Nous mangeons du poisson le vendredi.
column7: We eat fish on Fridays.
column8: Do not confuse it with «poison», which means poison (the toxic substance).

column6: Le brocoli est un légume vert.
column7: Broccoli is a green vegetable.
column8: It is masculine and very often used in the plural: les légumes.

column6: Je mange un fruit chaque jour.
column7: I eat a piece of fruit every day.
column8: It is often used in the plural: des fruits.

column6: Cette pomme est très rouge.
column7: This apple is very red.
column8: Pomme alone is the apple; the potato is pomme de terre.

column6: Il mange un œuf au petit-déjeuner.
column7: He eats an egg for breakfast.
column8: The plural is written œufs and pronounced ø: the f is silent.

column6: Nous mangeons du riz ce soir.
column7: We are eating rice tonight.
column8: The final z is silent.

column6: Vous voulez du sucre ?
column7: Do you want some sugar?
column8: It is masculine: le sucre. It is usually used with the partitive: du sucre.

column6: Pouvez-vous passer le sel ?
column7: Can you pass the salt?
column8: It is masculine: le sel.

column6: Je prends un café le matin.
column7: I have a coffee in the morning.
column8: It means both the drink and the place where you drink it.

column6: Elle boit du thé sans sucre.
column7: She drinks tea without sugar.
column8: It is written with an acute accent and pronounced te.

column6: Un jus d'orange, s'il vous plaît.
column7: An orange juice, please.
column8: The final s is silent and the plural is identical.

column6: Mon père aime le vin rouge.
column7: My father likes red wine.
column8: It is masculine: le vin. The final n marks a nasal vowel.

column6: Il commande une bière fraîche.
column7: He orders a cold beer.
column8: It is feminine: la bière.

column6: Ma mère fait un gâteau.
column7: My mother is making a cake.
column8: The plural is gâteaux. It is written with a circumflex.

column6: La soupe est encore chaude.
column7: The soup is still hot.
column8: It is feminine: la soupe.

column6: Je veux une salade verte.
column7: I want a green salad.
column8: It means both lettuce and the salad dish.

column6: Le repas est prêt.
column7: The meal is ready.
column8: The final s is silent and the plural is identical.

column6: Il met du beurre sur le pain.
column7: He puts butter on the bread.
column8: It is masculine: le beurre. It is used with the partitive: du beurre.

column6: Ce soir, nous mangeons du poulet.
column7: Tonight we are eating chicken.
column8: It means both the animal and its meat.

column6: Les enfants aiment le chocolat.
column7: Children love chocolate.
column8: The final t is silent.

column6: Notre maison est près du parc.
column7: Our house is near the park.
column8: Maison is the house as a building; a flat is an appartement.

column6: Ma chambre est très petite.
column7: My bedroom is very small.
column8: It usually means the bedroom.

column6: Elle prépare le dîner dans la cuisine.
column7: She is preparing dinner in the kitchen.
column8: It means both the room and the art of cooking.

column6: Nous regardons la télé dans le salon.
column7: We watch TV in the living room.
column8: It is masculine: le salon.

column6: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
column7: Close the door, please.
column8: It is feminine: la porte.

column6: La fenêtre est ouverte.
column7: The window is open.
column8: It is written with a circumflex.

column6: Le livre est sur la table.
column7: The book is on the table.
column8: It is feminine: la table.

column6: Il y a une chaise ici.
column7: There is a chair here.
column8: Chaise is the chair; an armchair is a fauteuil.

column6: Mon lit est très confortable.
column7: My bed is very comfortable.
column8: The final t is silent.

column6: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
column7: The children are playing in the garden.
column8: It is masculine: le jardin.

column6: Nous cherchons un appartement à Lyon.
column7: We are looking for a flat in Lyon.
column8: It is written with two p's and ends in -ment.

column6: Il y a un tableau sur le mur.
column7: There is a painting on the wall.
column8: Do not confuse it with mûr, which means ripe.

column6: Le toit de la maison est rouge.
column7: The roof of the house is red.
column8: It is masculine: le toit.

column6: L'escalier est à droite.
column7: The staircase is on the right.
column8: It is often used in the singular for the whole staircase.

column6: Où est ma clé ?
column7: Where is my key?
column8: It can also be spelled clef.

column6: J'allume la lampe du salon.
column7: I turn on the living room lamp.
column8: It is feminine: la lampe.

column6: Le chat dort sur le canapé.
column7: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
column8: It means sofa; in cooking a «canapé» is also a small party appetiser.

column6: Mes vêtements sont dans l'armoire.
column7: My clothes are in the wardrobe.
column8: It is feminine: l'armoire.

column6: Mon appartement est au deuxième étage.
column7: My flat is on the second floor.
column8: The ground floor is the rez-de-chaussée; the premier étage is the first floor above it.

column6: Je prends une douche le matin.
column7: I take a shower in the morning.
column8: It is feminine: la douche.

column6: Il y a un miroir dans l'entrée.
column7: There is a mirror in the hallway.
column8: It is masculine: le miroir.

column6: Le chat dort sur le tapis.
column7: The cat is sleeping on the rug.
column8: The final s is silent and the plural is identical.

column6: Nous mangeons sur le balcon.
column7: We eat on the balcony.
column8: It is masculine: le balcon.

column6: Mon voisin est très gentil.
column7: My neighbour is very nice.
column8: The feminine form is voisine.

column6: Le magasin ferme à sept heures.
column7: The shop closes at seven o'clock.
column8: False friend of English magazine: a magasin is a shop.

column6: Quel est le prix ?
column7: What is the price?
column8: The final x is silent and the plural is identical.

column6: Je n'ai pas d'argent.
column7: I have no money.
column8: It means both money and silver.

column6: Nous allons au marché le samedi.
column7: We go to the market on Saturdays.
column8: It is masculine: le marché.

column6: Elle porte un sac noir.
column7: She is carrying a black bag.
column8: It is masculine: le sac.

column6: Cette boutique vend des chaussures.
column7: This boutique sells shoes.
column8: It means a small shop.

column6: Vous payez à la caisse.
column7: You pay at the checkout.
column8: It is feminine: la caisse.

column6: Le client attend à la porte.
column7: The customer is waiting at the door.
column8: The feminine form is cliente.

column6: Le vendeur est très aimable.
column7: The shop assistant is very friendly.
column8: The feminine form is vendeuse.

column6: Ça coûte un euro.
column7: It costs one euro.
column8: The plural is euros.

column6: Je paie avec ma carte.
column7: I pay with my card.
column8: It also means a map and playing cards.

column6: Gardez le ticket, s'il vous plaît.
column7: Keep the receipt, please.
column8: It also means a simple ticket, for example for the metro.

column6: Ce vêtement est trop grand.
column7: This garment is too big.
column8: It is often used in the plural: les vêtements, clothes.

column6: Cette chaussure est trop petite.
column7: This shoe is too small.
column8: It is often used in the plural: les chaussures.

column6: Elle porte une robe bleue.
column7: She is wearing a blue dress.
column8: Robe is a woman's dress.

column6: Ce pantalon est trop long.
column7: These trousers are too long.
column8: In French it is singular: un pantalon.

column6: Il met une chemise blanche.
column7: He puts on a white shirt.
column8: It is feminine: la chemise.

column6: C'est un cadeau pour ma mère.
column7: It is a gift for my mother.
column8: The plural is cadeaux.

column6: Elle met les pommes dans le panier.
column7: She puts the apples in the basket.
column8: It is masculine: le panier.

column6: Nous faisons les courses au supermarché.
column7: We do the shopping at the supermarket.
column8: It is masculine: le supermarché.

column6: Excusez-moi, où est la gare ?
column7: Excuse me, where is the station?
column8: It only means a railway station; a bus station is a "gare routière".

column6: Je voudrais un billet pour Lyon.
column7: I would like a ticket to Lyon.
column8: It is used for train, plane and show tickets; "billet" also means a banknote.

column6: J'habite dans une grande ville.
column7: I live in a big city.
column8: It is always feminine; "en ville" means "in town" or "downtown".

column6: Le train part à huit heures.
column7: The train leaves at eight o'clock.
column8: You say "dans le train" for being inside it and "en train" for travelling by train.

column6: Mon avion arrive à midi.
column7: My plane arrives at noon.
column8: It is masculine: "un avion"; you travel "en avion".

column6: Ma valise est très lourde.
column7: My suitcase is very heavy.
column8: Faire sa valise means to pack one's suitcase.

column6: Nous faisons un voyage en Italie.
column7: We are taking a trip to Italy.
column8: It is masculine; "Bon voyage !" is the usual wish to someone leaving.

column6: Notre hôtel est près de la plage.
column7: Our hotel is near the beach.
column8: It is written with a circumflex accent and the h is silent.

column6: Ma voiture est devant la maison.
column7: My car is in front of the house.
column8: It is the everyday word for a car; "la voiture" is feminine.

column6: L'aéroport est loin du centre-ville.
column7: The airport is far from the city centre.
column8: It is masculine: "un aéroport".

column6: Quel est ton pays ?
column7: What is your country?
column8: The plural is identical: "les pays". It does not mean a village, which is "village".

column6: Ma rue est très calme.
column7: My street is very quiet.
column8: It means a street in a town; a road between towns is "la route".

column6: Le bus passe toutes les dix minutes.
column7: The bus comes every ten minutes.
column8: It is the short form of "autobus", and the final s is pronounced.

column6: Je prends un taxi pour la gare.
column7: I am taking a taxi to the station.
column8: It is spelled like the English word but pronounced the French way.

column6: Je prends le métro tous les jours.
column7: I take the subway every day.
column8: Métro is short for "métropolitain"; you say "en métro" for travelling by subway.

column6: Mon travail commence à neuf heures.
column7: My work starts at nine o'clock.
column8: The plural is "travaux", which often means roadworks or building works.

column6: Mon bureau est au deuxième étage.
column7: My office is on the second floor.
column8: It also means a desk; the plural is "bureaux".

column6: Mon patron est très gentil.
column7: My boss is very kind.
column8: The feminine is "patronne"; it is a normal, neutral word.

column6: La réunion commence à dix heures.
column7: The meeting starts at ten o'clock.
column8: It is feminine; it means a meeting, usually a work one.

column6: Quel est votre métier ?
column7: What is your profession?
column8: It means a trade or occupation; it is masculine.

column6: J'ai un ordinateur portable au bureau.
column7: I have a laptop computer at the office.
column8: In France the usual word is "ordinateur", not "computer".

column6: Je cherche un emploi à Paris.
column7: I am looking for a job in Paris.
column8: Emploi du temps means schedule; on its own "emploi" is a job.

column6: Notre équipe est très sympa.
column7: Our team is very nice.
column8: It is feminine and is used for work teams and sports teams.

column6: Nous avons un nouveau projet.
column7: We have a new project.
column8: It is masculine; the final t is silent.

column6: J'aime beaucoup la musique classique.
column7: I like classical music a lot.
column8: It is feminine and normally takes the definite article: "la musique".

column6: Ce film est très drôle.
column7: This film is very funny.
column8: It is masculine and the plural is "films".

column6: Le musée ouvre à dix heures.
column7: The museum opens at ten o'clock.
column8: It is masculine; the stress is on the last syllable.

column6: Nous allons au théâtre ce soir.
column7: We are going to the theatre tonight.
column8: It has a circumflex accent; "au théâtre" means "at the theatre".

column6: J'adore cette chanson française.
column7: I love this French song.
column8: It is feminine and means a song.

column6: Nous allons au cinéma samedi.
column7: We are going to the cinema on Saturday.
column8: It means both the art form and the building; it is masculine.

column6: Le français est une belle langue.
column7: French is a beautiful language.
column8: It also means the tongue in the mouth; it is always feminine.

column6: Mon père lit le journal le matin.
column7: My father reads the newspaper in the morning.
column8: The plural is irregular: "journaux". It can also mean a diary.

column6: Samedi, nous allons à une fête.
column7: On Saturday we are going to a party.
column8: It means a party or a public holiday; it has a circumflex accent.

column6: J'ai une grande famille.
column7: I have a big family.
column8: It is feminine; the "ill" is pronounced like a y sound.

column6: Cet enfant parle très bien.
column7: This child speaks very well.
column8: It is used for boys and girls: "un enfant", "une enfant"; here the dictionary article is masculine.

column6: Ce soir, nous allons au concert.
column7: Tonight we are going to a concert.
column8: It means a live concert; the final t is not pronounced, but the r is.

column6: Je fais du sport le dimanche.
column7: I do sport on Sundays.
column8: You say "faire du sport" to do sport.

column6: Ce jeu est très amusant.
column7: This game is very fun.
column8: The plural is "jeux", spelled with an x.

column6: Mon fils adore le football.
column7: My son loves football.
column8: In speech it is often shortened to "foot"; it means soccer, not American football.

column6: Les enfants jouent sur la plage.
column7: The children play on the beach.
column8: It is feminine; it has nothing to do with the English word "plague".

column6: Il y a une piscine dans l'hôtel.
column7: There is a swimming pool in the hotel.
column8: It is feminine: «la piscine». The «sc» is simply pronounced /s/.

column6: Paul est mon meilleur ami.
column7: Paul is my best friend.
column8: The feminine is "amie", which sounds the same.

column6: Je vais au travail en vélo.
column7: I go to work by bike.
column8: It is the everyday word for a bicycle; you can say "à vélo" or "en vélo".

column6: Nous faisons une promenade au parc.
column7: We are going for a walk in the park.
column8: You say "faire une promenade" or "se promener" to go for a walk.

column6: Je prends une photo de la plage.
column7: I am taking a photo of the beach.
column8: It is feminine because it is short for "photographie".

column6: Le dimanche, nous allons au parc.
column7: On Sundays we go to the park.
column8: The final c is not silent here; it is masculine.

column6: Ma sœur aime la danse.
column7: My sister likes dancing.
column8: It is feminine and means dance as an art or a single dance.

column6: Le match commence à huit heures.
column7: The match starts at eight o'clock.
column8: The plural is "matchs" or "matches"; it is a loanword from English.

column6: J'ai mal à la tête.
column7: I have a headache.
column8: You say "avoir mal à la tête" for a headache; it has a circumflex accent.

column6: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
column7: I am going to the doctor tomorrow.
column8: It often stays masculine even for a woman: "une femme médecin".

column6: Ma main gauche me fait mal.
column7: My left hand hurts.
column8: It is always feminine: "la main".

column6: J'ai mal au dos.
column7: I have a backache.
column8: The final s is silent; it means the back of the body.

column6: Mon ventre me fait très mal.
column7: My belly really hurts.
column8: It is masculine; "avoir mal au ventre" means to have a stomach ache.

column6: Il a mal au bras droit.
column7: He has a pain in his right arm.
column8: It is masculine, the final s is silent, and the plural is the same.

column6: Ma jambe est très fatiguée.
column7: My leg is very tired.
column8: It is feminine and is spelled with a j, not a g.

column6: Ma dent me fait très mal.
column7: My tooth hurts a lot.
column8: It is feminine; the final t is silent.

column6: Mon cœur bat très vite.
column7: My heart is beating very fast.
column8: It is written with the ligature œ; "avoir mal au cœur" means to feel nauseous.

column6: L'hôpital est à côté de la gare.
column7: The hospital is next to the station.
column8: The plural is irregular: "hôpitaux"; it has a circumflex accent.

column6: La pharmacie ferme à sept heures.
column7: The pharmacy closes at seven o'clock.
column8: In France a pharmacy is marked by a green cross; the word is feminine.

column6: La santé est très importante.
column7: Health is very important.
column8: It is also used as a toast: "Santé !".

column6: Mon fils a de la fièvre.
column7: My son has a fever.
column8: You say "avoir de la fièvre", with the partitive article.

column6: Je parle un peu français.
column7: I speak a little French.
column8: Parler takes "à" before the person: parler à quelqu'un.

column6: Nous mangeons du pain ici.
column7: We eat bread here.
column8: A -ger verb: the nous form is spelled "mangeons", with an extra e after the g.

column6: J'aime le café le matin.
column7: I like coffee in the morning.
column8: Aimer means both "to love" and "to like": j'aime le café is "I like coffee".

column6: Nous habitons dans une petite ville.
column7: We live in a small town.
column8: The h is silent: j'habite. You say habiter à Paris but habiter en France.

column6: Il travaille dans un bureau.
column7: He works in an office.
column8: Travailler means to work, not to travel (to travel is voyager).

column6: Nous regardons un film ce soir.
column7: We are watching a film tonight.
column8: Regarder takes its object directly, with no preposition: regarder la télé.

column6: Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît.
column7: I am looking for the station, please.
column8: Chercher takes its object directly, with no "for": chercher les clés.

column6: Nous achetons du pain tous les matins.
column7: We buy bread every morning.
column8: The stem changes: j'achète, but nous achetons.

column6: Ils aiment danser le samedi soir.
column7: They like dancing on Saturday night.
column8: A regular -er verb used without an object: elle danse bien.

column6: Elle chante sous la douche.
column7: She sings in the shower.
column8: A regular -er verb; the past participle is chanté.

column6: J'écoute de la musique le soir.
column7: I listen to music in the evening.
column8: Écouter takes its object directly, with no "to": écouter la radio.

column6: Elle étudie le français à l'université.
column7: She studies French at university.
column8: Étudier is used for studying a subject; "to learn" is apprendre.

column6: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
column7: The children play in the garden.
column8: You say jouer au football (sport) but jouer du piano (instrument).

column6: Nous marchons vingt minutes jusqu'au travail.
column7: We walk twenty minutes to work.
column8: Marcher also means "to work, to function": ça marche means "it works".

column6: Je donne le sel à Paul.
column7: I give the salt to Paul.
column8: Donner takes "à" before the person: donner quelque chose à quelqu'un.

column6: Elle porte une robe rouge.
column7: She is wearing a red dress.
column8: Porter means both "to wear" and "to carry".

column6: Je pense à mes amis.
column7: I am thinking about my friends.
column8: You say penser à quelqu'un; penser que introduces an opinion: je pense que oui.

column6: Je trouve mes clés sous le lit.
column7: I find my keys under the bed.
column8: Trouver also means "to think, to find": je trouve ça bon means "I find it good".

column6: J'aide ma mère à la cuisine.
column7: I help my mother in the kitchen.
column8: Aider takes the person directly: aider quelqu'un; before an infinitive it uses "à".

column6: Le train arrive à huit heures.
column7: The train arrives at eight o'clock.
column8: In the passé composé it takes être: je suis arrivé.

column6: Nous restons à la maison ce week-end.
column7: We are staying at home this weekend.
column8: Rester means "to stay, to remain"; in the passé composé it takes être: je suis resté.

column6: Je demande le prix au vendeur.
column7: I ask the seller the price.
column8: Demander takes "à" before the person: demander quelque chose à quelqu'un.

column6: Mon père aime cuisiner le dimanche.
column7: My father likes cooking on Sundays.
column8: Cuisiner means to prepare meals; la cuisine is also the kitchen (the room).

column6: Nous voyageons en train cet été.
column7: We are travelling by train this summer.
column8: A -ger verb: the nous form is spelled "voyageons".

column6: Je nage à la piscine le mardi.
column7: I swim at the pool on Tuesdays.
column8: A -ger verb: the nous form is spelled "nageons".

column6: Nous payons par carte.
column7: We pay by card.
column8: Payer has two possible conjugations: je paie or je paye.

column6: Elle utilise son téléphone pour travailler.
column7: She uses her phone to work.
column8: Utiliser is regular and corresponds to "to use" or "to utilise".

column6: Nous visitons le musée demain.
column7: We are visiting the museum tomorrow.
column8: Visiter is used for places; for people you say rendre visite à.

column6: Je téléphone à ma mère.
column7: I am phoning my mother.
column8: It takes "à" before the person: téléphoner à quelqu'un.

column6: Le cours commence à neuf heures.
column7: The class begins at nine o'clock.
column8: A -cer verb: the nous form is spelled "commençons", with a cedilla.

column6: Je prépare le dîner ce soir.
column7: I am preparing dinner tonight.
column8: Préparer un examen means to prepare for an exam.

column6: Je lave la voiture le samedi.
column7: I wash the car on Saturdays.
column8: For "to wash oneself" French uses the pronominal se laver; here the verb washes something.

column6: Le magasin ferme à sept heures.
column7: The shop closes at seven.
column8: Fermer is the opposite of ouvrir.

column6: J'oublie toujours mon parapluie.
column7: I always forget my umbrella.
column8: Before an infinitive it takes "de": oublier de fermer la porte.

column6: Je rencontre mes voisins dans l'escalier.
column7: I meet my neighbours on the stairs.
column8: Rencontrer often refers to meeting someone for the first time.

column6: Nous répétons la question.
column7: We repeat the question.
column8: The accent changes: je répète, but nous répétons.

column6: Il déteste faire la queue.
column7: He hates queueing.
column8: Détester can be followed directly by an infinitive: je déteste attendre.

column6: J'invite mes voisins à dîner.
column7: I invite my neighbours to dinner.
column8: It takes "à": inviter quelqu'un à dîner.

column6: Le livre tombe de la table.
column7: The book falls off the table.
column8: In the passé composé it takes être: je suis tombé.

column6: J'entre dans la cuisine.
column7: I come into the kitchen.
column8: Before a place it takes "dans": entrer dans la salle.

column6: Je rentre à la maison à six heures.
column7: I get home at six o'clock.
column8: Rentrer means to go back to where you started, usually home.

column6: Nous montons au deuxième étage.
column7: We go up to the second floor.
column8: It is also used for getting on a vehicle: monter dans le bus.

column6: Je passe devant la banque tous les jours.
column7: I pass the bank every day.
column8: Passer also means "to spend" time: passer une semaine à Paris.

column6: J'appelle le médecin demain.
column7: I am calling the doctor tomorrow.
column8: It doubles the l: j'appelle, but nous appelons.

column6: Elle coupe le pain avec un couteau.
column7: She cuts the bread with a knife.
column8: Couper takes its object directly: couper le pain.

column6: Je réserve une table pour ce soir.
column7: I book a table for tonight.
column8: Réserver means to book a table, a room or a ticket.

column6: Le professeur explique la leçon.
column7: The teacher explains the lesson.
column8: It takes "à" before the person: expliquer quelque chose à quelqu'un.

column6: Nous déjeunons à midi avec Paul.
column7: We have lunch at noon with Paul.
column8: Déjeuner is also a noun: le déjeuner means "lunch".

column6: Nous dînons souvent au restaurant.
column7: We often have dinner at a restaurant.
column8: Dîner is also a noun: le dîner means "dinner".

column6: Il gagne bien sa vie.
column7: He earns a good living.
column8: Gagner means both "to earn" and "to win": gagner un match.

column6: Nous allons être en retard.
column7: We are going to be late.
column8: Être is the most irregular verb: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes.

column6: Nous allons avoir faim.
column7: We are going to be hungry.
column8: Avoir is the auxiliary of most verbs in the passé composé: j'ai parlé.

column6: Je ne veux pas aller au bureau.
column7: I do not want to go to the office.
column8: Irregular (je vais, nous allons); it also forms the near future: je vais manger.

column6: Je ne veux pas faire de sport.
column7: I do not want to do any sport.
column8: Irregular (vous faites); also used for weather: il fait beau.

column6: Tu ne vas pas vouloir partir déjà ?
column7: You're not going to want to leave already?
column8: Je veux is very direct: to be polite say je voudrais.

column6: Je ne vais pas pouvoir venir demain.
column7: I will not be able to come tomorrow.
column8: Irregular (je peux, nous pouvons); it expresses ability and permission.

column6: Je ne veux pas savoir le prix.
column7: I do not want to know the price.
column8: Savoir is for facts and skills; for people and places use connaître.

column6: Elle ne veut pas venir au cinéma.
column7: She does not want to come to the cinema.
column8: Venir de + infinitive expresses the recent past: je viens de manger.

column6: Je ne peux pas voir la mer d'ici.
column7: I cannot see the sea from here.
column8: Irregular: je vois, nous voyons.

column6: Je ne veux pas prendre le bus.
column7: I do not want to take the bus.
column8: It is also used for eating and drinking: prendre un café, prendre le petit déjeuner.

column6: Je ne veux pas boire de café.
column7: I do not want to drink coffee.
column8: Irregular: je bois, nous buvons.

column6: Tu ne dois pas dire ça.
column7: You must not say that.
column8: Irregular: vous dites; it takes "à": dire quelque chose à quelqu'un.

column6: Nous ne finissons pas avant midi.
column7: We do not finish before noon.
column8: A regular -ir verb (nous finissons); before an infinitive it takes "de": finir de manger.

column6: Je ne choisis pas ce menu.
column7: I am not choosing this menu.
column8: A regular -ir verb: nous choisissons.

column6: Je ne veux pas partir demain.
column7: I do not want to leave tomorrow.
column8: Irregular (je pars, nous partons); partir means "to go away" and takes no direct object.

column6: Je ne peux pas dormir ce soir.
column7: I cannot sleep tonight.
column8: Irregular: je dors, nous dormons.

column6: Je ne veux pas lire ce livre.
column7: I do not want to read this book.
column8: Irregular: je lis, vous lisez.

column6: Je ne sais pas écrire ce mot.
column7: I do not know how to write this word.
column8: Irregular: j'écris, nous écrivons.

column6: Tu ne dois pas ouvrir cette fenêtre.
column7: You must not open this window.
column8: It ends in -ir but is conjugated like an -er verb: j'ouvre, tu ouvres.

column6: Je ne veux pas attendre le bus.
column7: I do not want to wait for the bus.
column8: Attendre does not mean "to attend"; it means "to wait for" and takes its object directly.

column6: Elle ne vend pas ses livres.
column7: She does not sell her books.
column8: A regular -re verb: je vends, nous vendons.

column6: Je ne peux pas comprendre la question.
column7: I cannot understand the question.
column8: It is conjugated like prendre: je comprends, nous comprenons.

column6: Je ne veux pas mettre de sucre.
column7: I do not want to put in sugar.
column8: Irregular: je mets, nous mettons; also used for "to put on": mettre un pull.

column6: Il ne veut pas apprendre l'allemand.
column7: He does not want to learn German.
column8: It is conjugated like prendre; before an infinitive it takes "à": apprendre à nager.

column6: Je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
column7: I do not want to go out tonight.
column8: Irregular like partir: je sors, nous sortons.

column6: Je ne veux pas répondre au téléphone.
column7: I do not want to answer the phone.
column8: It takes "à": répondre à une question; regular -re verb: je réponds.

column6: Je ne veux pas perdre mon billet.
column7: I do not want to lose my ticket.
column8: A regular -re verb: je perds, nous perdons.

column6: Je ne peux pas entendre la radio.
column7: I cannot hear the radio.
column8: Entendre means to perceive by ear; écouter is to listen on purpose.

column6: Je ne veux pas descendre ici.
column7: I do not want to get off here.
column8: A regular -re verb; without an object it takes être in the passé composé: je suis descendu.

column6: Tu ne vas pas devoir travailler demain.
column7: You will not have to work tomorrow.
column8: Irregular: je dois, nous devons; with a noun it also means "to owe": devoir dix euros.

column6: Elle ne peut pas connaître tout le monde.
column7: She can't know everyone.
column8: Used for people and places; for facts use savoir. Irregular: il connaît.

column6: Elle ne va pas recevoir de colis.
column7: She will not receive a parcel.
column8: Irregular with a cedilla: je reçois, but nous recevons.

column6: Mon frère est très grand.
column7: My brother is very tall.
column8: Means big for things and tall for people. The feminine is grande, and it usually comes before the noun.

column6: Nous avons un petit appartement.
column7: We have a small apartment.
column8: Feminine petite. It usually goes before the noun and its opposite is grand.

column6: Cette maison est très belle.
column7: This house is very beautiful.
column8: Feminine belle; before a vowel the masculine becomes bel. In il fait beau it describes the weather.

column6: J'habite dans un nouveau quartier.
column7: I live in a new neighbourhood.
column8: Feminine nouvelle; before a vowel the masculine becomes nouvel. Plural nouveaux. It usually goes before the noun.

column6: Ma voiture est très vieille.
column7: My car is very old.
column8: Feminine vieille; before a vowel the masculine becomes vieil. The masculine plural is the same as the singular: vieux.

column6: Ce gâteau est très bon.
column7: This cake is very good.
column8: Feminine bonne. Bon is an adjective; the matching adverb is bien.

column6: Ce film est mauvais.
column7: This film is bad.
column8: Feminine mauvaise. It is used for things and quality, and usually goes before the noun.

column6: Elle est heureuse avec sa famille.
column7: She is happy with her family.
column8: Feminine heureuse; the masculine plural stays heureux. The initial h is silent.

column6: Je suis content de te voir.
column7: I am glad to see you.
column8: Feminine contente. It is followed by de plus a verb or noun: content de.

column6: Les enfants sont fatigués ce soir.
column7: The children are tired this evening.
column8: Feminine fatiguée, plural fatigués. Do not confuse it with fatigant, which means tiring.

column6: L'eau de la douche est chaude.
column7: The shower water is hot.
column8: Feminine chaude. For a person you say avoir chaud, not être chaud.

column6: La soupe est froide.
column7: The soup is cold.
column8: Feminine froide. For weather you say il fait froid; for a person, avoir froid.

column6: Ces chaussures sont trop chères.
column7: These shoes are too expensive.
column8: Feminine chère. After the noun or with être it means expensive; before the noun it means dear.

column6: Le test est vraiment facile.
column7: The test is really easy.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural faciles. Its opposite is difficile.

column6: Cet exercice est assez difficile.
column7: This exercise is quite difficult.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural difficiles.

column6: Elle porte une robe rouge.
column7: She is wearing a red dress.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural rouges. Colour adjectives go after the noun.

column6: J'aime ton sac bleu.
column7: I like your blue bag.
column8: Feminine bleue, plural bleus. Colour adjectives go after the noun.

column6: Ma sœur est très jeune.
column7: My sister is very young.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural jeunes. It can go before the noun (un jeune homme).

column6: Le voyage en train est long.
column7: The train journey is long.
column8: Feminine longue (with a u), plural longs. It also describes time: un long voyage.

column6: Tu as une jolie maison.
column7: You have a pretty house.
column8: Feminine jolie, plural jolis. It usually goes before the noun.

column6: Ta mère est très gentille.
column7: Your mother is very kind.
column8: Feminine gentille, with two l's (pronounced with a y sound). It describes people.

column6: Mon chien est triste aujourd'hui.
column7: My dog is sad today.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural tristes.

column6: Mon fils est malade depuis lundi.
column7: My son has been ill since Monday.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. It can also be a noun: un malade (a patient).

column6: Tu es prêt pour l'examen.
column7: You are ready for the exam.
column8: Feminine prête. It sounds like près (near) but is spelled with a circumflex and a t.

column6: Cette place est libre.
column7: This seat is free.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. It means free as in available, not free of charge (that is gratuit).

column6: J'aime les pommes vertes.
column7: I like green apples.
column8: Feminine verte, plural verts. Colour adjectives go after the noun.

column6: Elle achète une chemise blanche.
column7: She is buying a white shirt.
column8: Feminine blanche, plural blancs. Colour adjectives go after the noun.

column6: Je bois mon café noir.
column7: I drink my coffee black.
column8: Feminine noire, plural noirs. Colour adjectives go after the noun.

column6: Le citron est jaune.
column7: The lemon is yellow.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural jaunes.

column6: Le train est très lent.
column7: The train is very slow.
column8: Feminine lente, plural lents. Its opposite is rapide.

column6: Cette voiture est rapide.
column7: This car is fast.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural rapides.

column6: Le frigo est plein.
column7: The fridge is full.
column8: Feminine pleine. The phrase plein de plus a noun means full of, lots of.

column6: Mon verre est vide.
column7: My glass is empty.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural vides. Its opposite is plein.

column6: Le magasin est ouvert le dimanche.
column7: The shop is open on Sundays.
column8: Feminine ouverte, plural ouverts. Its opposite is fermé.

column6: Le musée est fermé aujourd'hui.
column7: The museum is closed today.
column8: Feminine fermée, plural fermés. It is the past participle of fermer used as an adjective.

column6: Mes mains sont sales.
column7: My hands are dirty.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural sales. Its opposite is propre.

column6: Ce café est trop fort.
column7: This coffee is too strong.
column8: Feminine forte, plural forts. It applies to flavours, people and sounds.

column6: C'est un livre très intéressant.
column7: It is a very interesting book.
column8: Feminine intéressante, plural intéressants. It has an accented é and a double s.

column6: Ce sac est très léger.
column7: This bag is very light.
column8: Feminine légère (the accent changes), plural légers. Its opposite is lourd.

column6: Ma valise est trop lourde.
column7: My suitcase is too heavy.
column8: Feminine lourde, plural lourds. Its opposite is léger.

column6: Je ne parle pas allemand.
column7: I do not speak German.
column8: Before a vowel it becomes j' (j'ai, j'aime). It is not capitalised mid-sentence.

column6: Tu n'es pas fatigué ?
column7: Aren't you tired?
column8: Used with friends, family and children; with a stranger you normally use vous.

column6: Il n'aime pas le café.
column7: He does not like coffee.
column8: It also replaces masculine nouns for things (il = it): Le livre? Il est ici.

column6: Elle est dans la cuisine.
column7: She is in the kitchen.
column8: It also replaces feminine nouns for things (elle = it).

column6: Nous n'aimons pas le froid.
column7: We do not like the cold.
column8: Nous is rather formal; in speech on is often used instead.

column6: Vous avez une réservation ?
column7: Do you have a reservation?
column8: Used for one person you address politely and for several people. The verb is always plural.

column6: Ils ne travaillent pas le dimanche.
column7: They do not work on Sundays.
column8: Used for a male or mixed group. It sounds like il, but there is liaison before a vowel.

column6: Elles ne mangent pas de viande.
column7: They do not eat meat.
column8: Used only for a group of women or feminine nouns.

column6: On n'a pas de pain.
column7: We have no bread.
column8: In speech it means we, but the verb is third person singular. It can also be impersonal, like one.

column6: Ce livre n'est pas pour moi.
column7: This book is not for me.
column8: It is the stressed pronoun: used after a preposition or for emphasis.

column6: Qui est ce monsieur ?
column7: Who is this man?
column8: It is also a subject relative pronoun (that, who): la femme qui parle.

column6: Je ne suis pas très fatigué.
column7: I am not very tired.
column8: It goes before adjectives and adverbs, never directly before a verb (use beaucoup).

column6: Il est aussi content que nous.
column7: He is as pleased as we are.
column8: It means also, and in aussi ... que it means as ... as in comparisons.

column6: Je ne travaille pas ici.
column7: I do not work here.
column8: It shows the place where the speaker is; its opposite is là.

column6: Je ne dors pas bien.
column7: I do not sleep well.
column8: It is an adverb, so it never agrees. The matching adjective is bon.

column6: Elle ne danse pas mal.
column7: She does not dance badly.
column8: It is the opposite of bien. As a noun, avoir mal à means to have a pain in.

column6: Je ne mange pas beaucoup de viande.
column7: I do not eat much meat.
column8: Before a noun it is beaucoup de, with no article: beaucoup de temps.

column6: Nous avons peu de temps.
column7: We have little time.
column8: Peu de plus a noun means little or few; un peu de means a little.

column6: Il n'est pas toujours à l'heure.
column7: He is not always on time.
column8: It can also mean still (il travaille toujours). After pas in a negative it means not always.

column6: Je ne mange pas souvent de poisson.
column7: I do not often eat fish.
column8: It usually comes after the verb; in compound tenses it sits between the auxiliary and the participle.

column6: Je n'ai pas le temps maintenant.
column7: I do not have time now.
column8: It can go at the start or the end of a sentence.

column6: Je ne travaille pas aujourd'hui.
column7: I am not working today.
column8: It is one word even though it contains an apostrophe.

column6: Nous ne partons pas demain.
column7: We are not leaving tomorrow.
column8: It is also used in farewells: À demain! (see you tomorrow).

column6: Elle n'a pas travaillé hier.
column7: She did not work yesterday.
column8: It goes with past tenses: hier soir means last night.

column6: Tu as déjà mangé ce matin ?
column7: Have you already eaten this morning?
column8: In compound tenses it goes between the auxiliary and the past participle. It carries accents on both vowels.

column6: Nous ne dînons pas ensemble ce soir.
column7: We are not having dinner together tonight.
column8: As a noun it also means a set of things, but as an adverb it never changes.

column6: Il ne marche pas vite.
column7: He does not walk fast.
column8: It is an invariable adverb (not vitement). It is also used on its own: Vite!

column6: Il n'est pas à la maison.
column7: He is not at home.
column8: It merges with the articles: à + le = au, à + les = aux. It has a grave accent, unlike a (from avoir).

column6: Les clés ne sont pas dans mon sac.
column7: The keys are not in my bag.
column8: It shows being inside a space. With cities you use à, not dans.

column6: Le livre n'est pas sur la table.
column7: The book is not on the table.
column8: It is written without an accent, unlike sûr (sure).

column6: Le chat n'est pas sous le lit.
column7: The cat is not under the bed.
column8: Its opposite is sur. The final s is silent.

column6: Je ne voyage pas avec mes parents.
column7: I do not travel with my parents.
column8: The final c is pronounced. Its opposite is sans.

column6: Je ne bois pas mon café sans sucre.
column7: I do not drink my coffee without sugar.
column8: After sans the noun usually has no article: sans sucre, sans problème.

column6: Ce cadeau n'est pas pour toi.
column7: This gift is not for you.
column8: It shows recipient or purpose. After pour you use stressed pronouns (moi, toi).

column6: Il n'est pas chez lui.
column7: He is not at home.
column8: Used with a person or business: chez moi, chez le médecin. It has no single-word English equivalent.

column6: Elle n'attend pas devant la porte.
column7: She is not waiting in front of the door.
column8: Its opposite is derrière. It can also be an adverb (il passe devant).

column6: Le jardin n'est pas derrière la maison.
column7: The garden is not behind the house.
column8: Its opposite is devant. It has a grave accent on the second e and two r's.

column6: La gare n'est pas près d'ici.
column7: The station is not near here.
column8: It is usually près de plus a place. It sounds like prêt but is spelled differently.

column6: Elle n'aime pas la pluie et le froid.
column7: She does not like the rain and the cold.
column8: The final t is silent. It has no accent and is not the verb form est.

column6: Je ne comprends pas mais j'écoute.
column7: I do not understand but I am listening.
column8: It is spelled mais, which is not the same word as mes (my) or mai (May).

column6: Tu es à la maison ou au bureau ?
column7: Are you at home or at the office?
column8: It has no accent; with the accent (où) it means where.

column6: Je ne travaille pas quand je suis malade.
column7: I do not work when I am ill.
column8: It works both as a conjunction and as a question word: Quand pars-tu?

column6: Je ne viens pas si tu es malade.
column7: I am not coming if you are ill.
column8: Before il or ils it becomes s' (s'il pleut). It also means yes in answer to a negative question.

column6: Ma mère travaille à l'hôpital.
column7: My mother works at the hospital.
column8: «Maman» is the affectionate form, also used by adults.

column6: Mon père habite à Lyon.
column7: My father lives in Lyon.
column8: «Papa» is the affectionate form; «père» is more neutral.

column6: Mon frère joue au football.
column7: My brother plays football.
column8: For «brothers and sisters» you say «frères et sœurs».

column6: Ma sœur étudie à Paris.
column7: My sister studies in Paris.
column8: It is written with the joined letter «œ», not «oe».

column6: Cet homme parle très vite.
column7: This man speaks very fast.
column8: The h is silent: «l'homme» sounds like «lom».

column6: Cette femme est médecin.
column7: This woman is a doctor.
column8: It is pronounced «fam»; it means both woman and wife.

column6: Quel jour sommes-nous aujourd'hui ?
column7: What day is it?
column8: Do not confuse it with «journée»: «jour» is the day as a date, «journée» as a length of time.

column6: Tu as l'heure, s'il te plaît ?
column7: Do you have the time, please?
column8: «Quelle heure est-il ?» means «what time is it?»; the h is silent.

column6: L'école commence à huit heures.
column7: School starts at eight o'clock.
column8: It is feminine and written with an acute accent.

column6: Mon téléphone est sur la table.
column7: My phone is on the table.
column8: A mobile phone is called «portable» in France.

column6: Le chat dort sur le canapé.
column7: The cat sleeps on the sofa.
column8: The female cat is «chatte»; the final t is silent.

column6: Mon chien aime jouer dehors.
column7: My dog likes playing outside.
column8: The female dog is «chienne».

column6: Quel est votre nom ?
column7: What is your surname?
column8: It mostly means the surname; the first name is «prénom».

column6: Ce restaurant est près de la gare.
column7: This restaurant is near the station.
column8: The final t is silent.

column6: Je ne m'appelle pas Paul, je m'appelle Marc.
column7: My name is not Paul, my name is Marc.
column8: It is written with an apostrophe; «je m'appelle…» is how you introduce yourself. «Appelle» has two l.

column6: Comment est ta nouvelle maison ?
column7: How is your new house?
column8: On its own, «Comment ?» asks someone to repeat.

column6: Pourquoi est-il si fatigué ?
column7: Why is he so tired?
column8: It is written as one word; the answer starts with «parce que».
